title: A note on exploiting structure when using slack variables
contribution: Shows that, when inequalities are converted with slack variables and solved by an augmented-Lagrangian method, the Newton/model linear algebra can be reduced from order n+m to order n by eliminating the slacks in closed form, and that reduced-space descent lifts to full-space descent for iterative solvers.
problem_entry: Weakness in the authors' own code: LANCELOT's SBMIN treats slacks like problem variables, so linear algebra is O(n+m) when m >> n, e.g. discretized semi-infinite constraints (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Block-triangular factorization (3.4) of the free-variable Newton system cancels the A_{Iy,Ix} terms, so only the n_i x n_i matrix B_{Ix,Ix} + rho A_{Ay,Ix}^T A_{Ay,Ix} is factorized (3.8) and the slack step is recovered explicitly (3.9); for iterative solvers the reduced descent condition (3.10) suffices (pp. 7-8).
assumptions: Augmented Lagrangian with bounds kept out of Phi; structured Hessian approximation (1.7); active set fixed at the base point (its choice out of scope); derivatives evaluated at (x,y); convex model needs the reduced matrix positive definite (pp. 3-8).
proof_devices: block elimination whose Schur complement after the slack pivots is exactly the reduced matrix (4.1), so rho A^T A terms cancel in exact arithmetic (pp. 7-9)

descent lift: full directional derivative = reduced one - mu ||lambda^b_Iy||^2 (3.11); convexity of Psi with Psi(0)=0 gives the reduced descent condition for any descent method started at 0, e.g. truncated CG (3.12)-(3.13) (p. 8)
cost comparison via eigenvalue interlacing after block elimination (spectrum of (3.4) wider than that of (4.1)) (p. 9)
experiments: none; the LANCELOT speed-up is stated as a belief (p. 9)
positioning: Slacks standard in LP (Dantzig, Murtagh, Chvatal) and NLP (Murtagh-Saunders); the trick apparently used but unpublicized in MINOS; compares work per iteration with barrier / Lagrangian-barrier methods (pp. 3-4, 9).
writing: Short 'note' genre: one-sentence abstract, derivation chosen to 'emphasize the reduction in computational effort', an itemized Discussion of costs of not exploiting structure, and thanks to a referee whose report was almost as long as the manuscript (pp. 3, 7-9).
limits_future: No numerical results; active-set strategy deferred to the literature; future: exploit the structure in LANCELOT, especially when m >> n (pp. 6, 9).

method_links.note: Structure of slack variables exploited in the linear algebra; structured Hessian approximation keeps first-derivative structure and approximates only second-order terms.
Algebra tied to the authors' released code (SBMIN options) but no numbers; the performance claim is a stated belief; a self-review of the package rather than a triad.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Short note names a specific inefficiency of the authors' released LANCELOT/SBMIN linear algebra and gives the fix.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Slack variables separated from problem variables and eliminated in closed form; also in S032 (Boolean/continuous/integer) and S141 (logical vs ordinary constraints); overlaps Method 5 step 4.

transferable: Eliminate auxiliary variables that enter the Hessian through an identity block by block-triangular factorization; factorize only the Schur complement in the original variables and recover the auxiliary step by formula (p. 7).
Justify a reduced-space inexact inner solver by showing the full directional derivative of the recovered step equals the reduced one plus a nonpositive term (p. 8).

Argue a reduction on four separate costs: dimension, symbolic-factorization memory (exact cancellations invisible to symbolic analysis), Krylov convergence via eigenvalue interlacing, and finite-termination count (pp. 8-9).

quotes.text: However, if slack variables are handled explicitly, we shall show that the linear algebra need only involve matrices of order O(n).
The description given here is intended to emphasize the reduction in computational effort possible when the structure inherent in the linear system (3.3) is properly exploited.

title: Removing clouds and recovering ground observations in satellite image sequences via temporally contiguous robust matrix completion
contribution: Proposes a two-stage cloud-removal method (dark-channel cloud detection, then TECROMAC: l1 data fit on detected clear pixels + nuclear norm + temporal smoothness) with two ALM-based solvers, and shows it recovers frames that are entirely cloud-covered, where MC and RMC fail.
problem_entry: Application limit: clouds limit satellite imagery; MC/RMC need some clear pixels in every image and fail on fully covered frames (tropics up to 90% of the time); prior methods need masks or non-optical sensors (pp. 1-2, 4).
key_idea: Start from an ideal rank-minimization model with a disagreement budget and a temporal-smoothness budget and replace each piece by a convex surrogate: ||P_Omega(Y-X)||_1 + lambda1 ||X||_* + (lambda2/2)||XR||_F^2, solved by ALM with inexact proximal gradient (SVT) or SVD-free alternating factorized gradients (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Low rank (few land types), sparse detector errors, temporal continuity (p. 3); majorizer needs cI >= AA^T = H (p. 5); no convergence or recovery guarantee stated; heuristic white-background post-processing, fails with heavy snow (p. 3).
proof_devices: majorize-minimize: Q(X, Xhat) = F(X) + (c/2)||X - Xhat||^2 - (1/2)||(X - Xhat)A||^2 >= F(X), completing the square gives an SVT step on a gradient step (p. 5)
nuclear-norm factorization identity ||X||_* = min (1/2)(||U||^2 + ||V||^2) for an SVD-free scheme (p. 6)
closed-form E-update by soft thresholding (eq. 9, p. 6)
experiments: Synthetic clouds on 3 background-modelling videos, relative reconstruction error vs MC, RMC, interpolation and TECMAC (ablation), one fixed parameter set; IPG vs ALT time/accuracy; real MODIS 181 images judged visually (pp. 6, 8).
positioning: Origin in RPCA and matrix completion; property table vs interpolation, MC, RMC; RPCA/SPCP directly on cloudy data said to usually fail under dense cloud; footnote contrasts ML-style ALM updates with optimizers' practice citing CGT 1991 (pp. 2, 4-5).
writing: Numbered improvement list in the introduction, property table (Table 1), ideal formulation before convex surrogate, strong conclusion wording (superior performance) (pp. 1, 3-4, 8).
limits_future: Heuristic detector and snow limitation admitted; real-data evaluation visual only; no future work stated (pp. 3, 8).

method_links.note: Augmented-Lagrangian machinery (CGT 1991 cited) carried into robust matrix completion; variant: ML-style ALM updating both multipliers and penalty each iteration, flagged in a footnote.
Weak: application-first paper in the users' venue (CVPR); no account of a user or partner in the text.
Weak: low-rank and temporal-smoothness structure encoded in the model.
Three synthetic videos, one visual real case and one parameter setting support a 'superior performance' claim (also Taste warning signs 3 and 6); Conn is a middle author, so not attributable to him.

transferable: Write the ideal combinatorial model (rank, counting budget, smoothness budget) first, then replace each nonconvex piece by its convex surrogate term by term (pp. 3-4).
Use a method-by-assumption property table to show which baselines violate which modelling assumption (Table 1, p. 4).
Include the model minus one term as a baseline (TECMAC) to justify that term (p. 8).
Derive a proximal step for quadratic + nuclear norm objectives from a majorizer with cI >= H and completion of the square (p. 5).
coauthors: J. Wang, P. A. Olsen, A. C. Lozano

quotes.text: Mathematical optimizers would only update one or the other
Tropical regions for example can be completely covered by clouds as often as 90% of the time.

title: An ADMM based framework for automl pipeline configuration
contribution: Formulates joint algorithm selection and hyper-parameter optimization as a mixed continuous-integer black-box program and uses ADMM to split it into small continuous black-box HPO, closed-form integer projection and bandit-based algorithm selection, with black-box constraints handled by slacks in the augmented Lagrangian; outperforms Auto-sklearn and TPOT on 15/30 datasets.
problem_entry: AutoML CASH seen as mixed continuous-integer black-box NLP with coupled algorithm choice and hyper-parameters, no gradients, plus deployment/fairness black-box constraints that penalty approaches cannot guarantee (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Explicit Boolean selection variables and a projection-based continuous surrogate with a consensus equality let ADMM decompose the problem so that black-box search runs only over the small active set of continuous variables (<15 vs about 100), since DFO cost grows with dimension; black-box inequalities become equalities with bounded slacks (pp. 2-5).
assumptions: No convergence guarantee (ADMM theory needs convexity/smoothness, violated here); conditional hyper-parameters flattened; artificial objective encodes assumed properties: deterministic, nonconvex, possibly discontinuous, conditional, locally stable in theta, sequential (pp. 2, 5, 27).
proof_devices: projection surrogate f~(theta~) = f(P_D(theta~)) plus consensus constraint theta~ = delta in D to make operator splitting over mixed variables well defined (p. 3)
bounded slack reformulation g_i - eps_i + u_i = 0, u_i in [0, eps_i] for black-box constraints (p. 4)
Thompson sampling for combinatorial bandits with probabilistic (Bernoulli-converted) rewards (Alg. A1, p. 13)
experiments: 30 UCI/OpenML/Kaggle binary datasets, 1 - AUROC, 1 hour x 10 trials, vs vanilla Auto-sklearn, TPOT50, random search with parity rules; constrained Kaggle case (CST vs post-hoc-filtered UCST); splitting ablation vs joint BO (up to 153x speedup); sensitivity and cheap artificial objective; cost unit wall-clock time (pp. 5-8, 20-27).
positioning: Against SMBO (SMAC, TPE, GP-BO), Hyperband/BOHB, meta-learning and toolkits (Auto-WEKA, Auto-sklearn, TPOT, ML-Plan, AlphaD3M); differs from prior ADMM + gradient-free work (ZO ADMM, ADMMBO); cites Conn-Scheinberg-Vicente 2009 as a possible sub-solver (pp. 1-2, 4-5).
writing: Numbered contributions with section pointers and quantified claims; 'not a single algorithm but a framework' framing; explicit parity section in appendix; two numerical inconsistencies (27%/20% swapped between p. 1 and p. 6; d_I 0.07 vs 0.7) (pp. 1, 5-6, 21).
limits_future: No convergence theory; binary classification only; no single best sub-solver; comparison acknowledged to favour TPOT; no future work stated (pp. 5, 7, 15, 21).

method_links.note: Variables separated by type and each block given its natural solver; only the active set enters black-box HPO, justified by DFO's dimension-dependent evaluation cost.
Augmented Lagrangian/operator splitting carried into AutoML; slack + AL treatment of black-box constraints mirrors S089; DFO book cited as sub-solver.
Code and numbers without a convergence theorem, openly stated.
Public datasets, parity protocol, ablations and 10 trials, but cost unit is wall-clock time, not evaluations; cheap artificial objective isolates optimizer overhead.

title: The continuous quadrant penalty formulation of logical constraints
contribution: Replaces binary big-M/complementary formulations of a conditional constraint by a smooth nonconvex piecewise-quadratic penalty on the open fourth quadrant of (t(x), f(x)), proves it is an S-repulsive penalty after impossibility results fix its minimal form, and shows local NLP solves find conflict-free aircraft maneuvers on 35 benchmark instances in seconds.
problem_entry: Logical constraints normally need a binary per constraint (big-M instability, complementary nonlinearity); asks whether continuous optimization can handle them, explicitly answering Conn's 1981 question on penalty functions in discrete/global optimization (pp. 2-4, 13).
key_idea: Map t > 0 => f >= 0 to (t,f) outside the open fourth quadrant S and penalize only S with a function that is zero off S, positive on S, continuous and 'leans outwards' (every descent direction exits S); unique 3-piece PL g_alpha is nonsmooth, so construct a 4-piece smooth piecewise quadratic g_beta (beta = 3) (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: t, f real-valued functions of x; only logical constraints penalized, others to NLP solver; nonconvex penalty and feasible set, so local infeasibility possible and global guarantees need global optimization; feasibility problems only (pp. 2-4, 11, 13).
proof_devices: impossibility results bound the design space: no convex S-violation dipstick when complement nonconvex (Prop. 2), no two-piece PL dipstick unless S is a half-space (Prop. 3), at least four pieces for a smooth piecewise quadratic (pp. 4-7)
uniqueness via the Conn-Mongeau 1998 lemma that gradient jumps across a PL ridge are multiples of the ridge normal (Prop. 4, p. 5)
'leans outwards' by case analysis on the active gradient piece with explicit threshold step gamma = -t/d1 or -f/d2 (Props. 7-8, pp. 6, 9)
positivity by restriction to transverse lines f = t - 2X and endpoint evaluation of a concave quadratic, 4X^2/(beta+1)^2 > 0 (pp. 8-9)
C^1 by gradient matching on the four boundary lines (p. 9)
experiments: Aircraft conflict avoidance (speed + heading), 35 Random Circle Problem instances with 10-30 aircraft, AMPL + IPOPT 3.12 with multistart: zero penalty on all instances, second start on 2, mean CPU 0.23/1.05/3.68 s, max 20.06 s; no direct MINLP comparison, bounds help B&B in [5] (pp. 10-12).
positioning: Against big-M and complementary MINLP formulations (Belotti et al.); relaxations out of scope; lineage from Conn's 1971 thesis, 1973 l1 penalty, Pietrzykowski, 1981 NATO question, Gamble-Conn-Pulleyblank 1991 and Conn-Mongeau 1998; Pinar-Zenios smoothing rejected (convex only) (pp. 3-7).
writing: Abstract opens with a question; evocative named definitions ('S-violation dipstick', 'leans outwards'); figures of restrictions to lines; honest 'not directly comparable' framing of results; posthumous dedication (pp. 2, 4-6, 12).
limits_future: Only feasibility problems; penalty weight vs original objective left open; local solutions via multistart; one application; future: other problems with many binaries (pp. 12-13).

method_links.note: Conn's penalty-function machinery (1971-1981) and Conn-Mongeau PL theory carried into logical/discrete constraints; the paper's own framing.
Only logical constraints penalized, others handled exactly by IPOPT; closest-approach reformulation exploits problem structure.
Air-traffic application in the variant closest to operational constraints; instance sizes compared with controllers' practice.
Theory + numbers with off-the-shelf AMPL/IPOPT instead of a new code (consistent with Heuristic 8).

This work is in the spirit of the questioning of Conn as to whether penalty functions can have a significant impact in discrete or global optimization.
